name: Sunbed + MT2 stack
lead: The sunbed plus MT2 stack is a looksmaxxing practice that pairs indoor tanning sessions with melanotan II (MT2), an unlicensed synthetic analogue of the hormone alpha-MSH, to build a deep tan faster than either would alone. Users want darker, more even skin colour, which many in these communities say adds contrast, definition and a healthier, more attractive look.[1][2][6]

Melanotan II stimulates melanin production, and its reversible effects include darkening of moles and freckles, flushing, nausea and, in men, erections. It has never been approved as a medicine, and unlicensed products are sold online and in some gyms and salons.[1] Indoor tanning devices emit mostly UVA with a little UVB; improving appearance is the most commonly cited reason people tan indoors.[2]

Health agencies have warned against unlicensed melanotan since 2007, and the World Health Organization classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen. Wikipedia notes that reported melanomas in melanotan users coincided with heavy sunbathing and sunbed use, and that a 2021 review said higher melanoma rates among users probably reflect greater UV exposure.[1][2] No clinical trial of the combination has been published.

angle.text: Practitioners combine an unlicensed melanin-stimulating peptide with UV tanning to reach a darker complexion sooner, wanting more contrast, a leaner-looking face and an even colour.

infobox: Health agencies since 2007 (MT2); WHO Group 1 carcinogen (UV)[1][2]

paras: The stack is the combination of two separate practices. Melanotan II acts on melanocortin receptors to increase melanin and may increase sexual arousal through MC4 receptor activation.[1] Sunbeds darken existing melanin with UVA and, through their small UVB output, stimulate new melanin.[2] Users describe the pairing as a way to need fewer or shorter sunbed sessions, a belief that rests on community reports rather than trials.[6]

Scientists at the University of Arizona developed melanotan I and II in the 1980s as possible sunless tanning agents. Melanotan I (afamelanotide) was licensed to an Australian start-up that became Clinuvel, and the FDA approved afamelanotide in 2019 for a rare genetic sun sensitivity. Melanotan II was licensed for sexual dysfunction research but never approved; Palatin stopped development in 2000 and moved to bremelanotide, approved by the FDA in 2019.[1]

Agencies in Norway (December 2007), Denmark (2008), the UK (2008), Ireland (February 2009) and the FDA (a warning letter in January 2009) issued warnings about unlicensed products, citing legality, case reports and possible impurities.[1]

Friedrich Wolff invented the sunbed in 1975, and salons spread across Europe and North America in the late 1970s.[2] High-pressure beds can deliver 10 to 15 times the UVA of midday sun.[2] A 2022 review described sunbed exposure as having well-documented harms and no clear benefit beyond cosmetic outcomes.[3]

Wikipedia reports a relative melanoma risk of 1.20 for ever-users and 1.59 for those who began before age 35 (2012 analysis), and notes links to skin ageing, burns and eye damage.[2] A BMJ meta-analysis estimated the melanoma burden attributable to sunbed use in western Europe.[4] Regulation includes Brazil's 2009 ban on cosmetic use and Australia's 2015 ban on commercial tanning.[2]

No studies found on the combination. Studies of sunbeds alone are observational and meta-analytic, for example a 2012 BMJ systematic review of melanoma attributable to sunbed use and a 2019 review on sunbeds and melanoma risk.[4][5] For melanotan II, Wikipedia cites a 2013 review finding no conclusive evidence it causes melanoma, a 2021 review attributing higher melanoma risk among users to greater UV exposure, and a 2020 in vivo study in which it suppressed melanoma progression.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sunbed use is debated as a way to improve looks, with posters weighing short-term appearance against cancer risk.[6][7][8]

claims.claim: Sunbed tanning improves looks, especially for women
claims.believers: One poster said it "makes u look better shortterm" but that side effects are heavy; another said it suits women only.[6]
claims.experts: Reviews describe sunbed exposure as carrying well-documented harms with no clear benefit beyond cosmetic outcomes.[3]

claims.claim: A weekly sunbed session is a basic essential, with extra benefits
claims.believers: A user planned a weekly 20-minute high-intensity session, hoping for a tan and a testosterone and muscle boost; another called 20 minutes of sun weekly essential.[8]
claims.experts: No studies found support testosterone or muscle effects from sunbeds; the 2022 review lists skin cancers, premature ageing, burns and eye damage.[3]

claims.claim: One sunbed session can lead to skin cancer
claims.believers: A user posted that he got skin cancer after his first ever sunbed session; others replied with supplement suggestions such as beta carotene.[7]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses show a higher melanoma risk with ever-use, rising with early first use.[2][4]

card.summary: Pairing unlicensed melanotan with tanning beds to rush pigment; two documented-risk exposures and no trial of the combination.
card.note: Combines an unlicensed peptide with a Group 1 carcinogen exposure.

quick.overview:
The stack combines melanotan II, an unlicensed tanning peptide, with tanning bed sessions to darken skin faster. It circulates in looksmaxxing tanning discussions.

No studies were found testing the combination.
quick.mechanism: Melanotan II mimics alpha-MSH to stimulate melanin production, while UV light triggers tanning directly. Proponents expect the two to add together; this has not been studied.
quick.risks: Melanotan II is unlicensed and regulators warn against it. UV tanning devices are classified as carcinogenic and linked to higher melanoma risk; reviews note melanoma reports in melanotan users may reflect extra UV exposure.
